findings.what: On all seven puzzles the right answer is the first button, so after two screens the position gives the answer away. Vary where the right answer sits.

The lamps are drawn always lit, with their star point wired straight to the hull. Yet the monitor's DC trace and its reading skip that path. In reality a set of filament lamps is a path to the hull of around a kilohm (computed for small lamps at 254 V), which would pull the monitor below every alarm level. That is why lamps are switched in only to test. Add a press-to-test switch in the lamps' common lead, or a sentence on screen 1. Also correct the ignores note, which says the lamps only "pull the voltages a little".

The motion drags the capacitance from 1 to 10 µF a phase for ten drives. Each drive's filter is tens of nanofarads, 10 to 100 nF in the brief, so ten of them add roughly 0.1 to 1 µF. That makes the effect look ten or more times too big. Step to about 2 µF, or change the premise to ten drives plus a long new cable run.

findings.where: Screen 9, explain, contested block and the finish line
findings.what: The class rule's 50 Ω/V is the point the alarm must sound by, so it is a floor. The makers' 100 and 500 Ω/V are higher settings that still meet it. Framing this as "guidance disagrees" teaches a contest when the real point is a minimum and how far above it to set. Say that in one sentence, and keep the trade: higher settings warn sooner but alarm on a big or damp system.

findings.where: Screen 9 and explain, "A maker advises about 100 Ω/V" and "Some call 500 Ω/V typical"
findings.what: These sentences say who holds a figure instead of what the setting does, which breaks the plain-writing rule. Say what each level is for (the rule's minimum, a common setting, an early warning) and leave the source names in the footnotes.

The readouts show L2 as the dimmest lamp (248 V) and L3 as the brightest (261 V), while the faulted L1 stays at 254 V, and the words never explain it. The step that the capacitance on all three phases holds the hull at the star point is also skipped. Swap the repeated "The reading sits below even the lowest path" for one sentence: a weak fault on a capacitive system nudges the hull sideways, so the dim lamp can point to the wrong phase. That keeps the screen at about 90 words.
"Now switch on Damp everywhere" tells him to act, but the demonstration has already switched it on. Write "Damp everywhere is now on."
The read sentence is 29 words with a "while" clause. Split it into two sentences.

The demonstration quietly switches Damp everywhere off, so the dial climbs from 20 to 500 kΩ, and the words never mention it. It also shows only one slow settle, so "the slower the dial settles" has nothing on screen to compare with. Let the dial settle once at 1 µF and then at 5 µF, or name the drying in the words.

Until Check is pressed the needle sits still at 0 kΩ, below the alarm line, with the alarm lamp off and the readout stuck on "Settling". That reads as a dead short that does not alarm. Open the screen at the settled 500 kΩ, or keep the needle creeping.
At the opening level of 44 kΩ the dashed alarm line sits almost on the "50" tick. That invites mixing it up with 50 Ω/V. Label the line with its kΩ value.

findings.where: Dial while settling (360 light and dark, moved state)
findings.what: While the dial creeps, the needle can sit below the amber alarm line with the alarm lamp still off. A small "measuring" mark beside the lamp would explain why it has not lit yet.

"After a change, the dial now takes longer to settle" reads awkwardly. Try "Now the dial takes longer to settle after every change." The hint for "Their filters lower the insulation resistance" just repeats the right answer. A better hint: lower resistance would change the reading, and if anything make it settle faster.

findings.where: Footnotes across the lesson (screens 1, 3, 5, 9, 11 and the practice)
findings.what: The lesson carries eight footnotes, three of them on consecutive sentences on screen 9. Keep the ones on alarm levels and rules, and drop [^2] and [^3], which mark explanations rather than values he would look up.
At 360 px the three lamps' halos and rays run into each other, which crowds the L1, L2 and L3 labels. Space the lamps a few pixels further apart or shorten the rays.
